title: Charging for this without underselling yourself
promise: You'll put a price on what you know how to do: what gets charged, how to quote without falling short, and what maintenance includes. By the end you'll have your proposal written with three figures.
why: Álvaro was asked to build the booking assistant for another clinic. He said «I'll do it for $350» because it had taken him a weekend. It took him three weeks: meetings to understand their situation, their odd opening hours, two people who had to be trained, and then four months of phone calls every time something broke. He charged $350 for around forty hours. His mistake wasn't setting a low price: it was quoting what it had cost him to build it, not what it costs to build it for someone else.

theory.title: You don't charge for the build, you charge for the problem solved
theory.text: The first instinct is to work out the hours it takes you and multiply by what you think your hour is worth. That's the direct route to being underpaid, because your hours go down as you get better: the better you are, the less you charge. The other way to look at it is what it's worth to whoever receives it. If a clinic saves twenty calls a day, that's hours of someone's time each month, and that number doesn't change because you built it quickly. The price sits somewhere between what it costs you to do and what it saves them, and to know where you need both figures. Most people only know the first.
theory.analogy: A plumber doesn't charge for the half hour it takes to change the washer. They charge for you no longer having a leak. And you don't argue about their hourly rate.
theory.example: Álvaro's assistant saves about two hours of reception a day. That's forty hours a month. He charged $350 for solving it permanently.

theory.title: What it's going to cost you isn't what it cost you
theory.text: Building it for yourself was cheap because you knew your own case, your own data and your own quirks, and you could leave it half-finished with no consequences. Building it for someone else includes four things that weren't there the first time: understanding their situation, adapting it to their particulars, training whoever will use it, and being available when it breaks. On projects like this, those four take longer than building. The practical rule plenty of people use and that works: work out what you think it'll take and multiply by three. The first time you do it, it'll look like an exaggeration; after two projects you'll be falling short.
theory.example: Álvaro estimated a weekend. It was forty hours. Three times his estimate would have been twenty-four, still short, but in a different order of magnitude.

theory.title: Quoting in three parts avoids nearly every argument
theory.text: A quote that works has three separate figures, and separating them is what prevents the disputes. First: the set-up, a one-off payment for leaving it working. Second: the monthly cost of the tools, which isn't yours, it's theirs, and goes in their name. And third: maintenance, a monthly amount for watching it and fixing breakdowns. Mixing them is what leads to someone calling you at nine at night in three months' time about a breakdown they believed was included in the price. And the second always has to be stated, even though it isn't your money, because if it appears as a surprise on their invoice they'll come to you about it.
theory.example: «Set-up: $1,400 one-off. Tools: about $30 a month in your name. Maintenance: $110 a month, includes a monthly review and breakdowns fixed within 48 hours.»

theory.title: Writing what it doesn't include, in the same size type
theory.text: The quote that causes trouble isn't the one that charges too little: it's the one that doesn't say where it ends. You have to write what it doesn't include, and write it in the same size type as the price. New features, changes of scope, training more people than agreed, integrating with another system that turns up later, migrating to another tool. Each of those is a separate quote, and saying so from the start doesn't frighten anyone off: on the contrary, it gives the impression you know what you're talking about. What frightens people off is discovering it halfway through.
theory.example: «Doesn't include: changes to the workflow once approved, integration with your management software, or training new staff after the first three months. Each is quoted separately.»

theory.title: The same thing sold twice is worth double and costs half
theory.text: Here's the difference between charging by the hour and building something that grows. The first time you build a system like this it costs you forty hours. The second, if you've done the handover package from lesson 45, it costs you ten: you already have the workflows, the instructions, the checks and the answers to the usual questions. You can charge something similar and take a quarter of the time. That's the real reason for packaging a project, and it isn't elegance: it's that a good handover turns a job into a product. Which is why it pays to pick one kind of client and repeat, rather than doing something different every time.
theory.example: Álvaro, after the clinic, built the same thing for two more: physiotherapy, podiatry and a beauty salon. The wording and the opening hours changed; the setup was the same.

theory.title: When to say no
theory.text: Some jobs work out expensive even when they pay well, and it's worth recognising them beforehand. When the client isn't clear what problem they want solved; when they ask for something needing sensitive data you can't handle; when the price only works if you do the support hours for free; or when whoever decides isn't whoever will use it. That last is the most treacherous: you build what the boss asked for, nobody uses it, and the blame ends up being yours. Saying no in time, or turning the job into a small paid first phase to define the problem properly, is what separates working from firefighting.
theory.example: «Before the full project, I propose two diagnostic sessions for $230 to define exactly what gets automated. If we go ahead afterwards, they come off the total.»

tasks.title: Work out what you save them
tasks.action: Take the number you measured in lesson 46 and turn it into time or money per month. How many times a day that thing you solve happens, how many minutes each time, how many days a month. Multiply and convert to hours. If you know what that hour costs there, convert to money. This is the number that holds your price up.
tasks.expect: One figure: hours or money saved per month. If it comes out small, that's valuable information: perhaps that project shouldn't be sold, or should be sold on some ground other than saving.
tasks.stuck: If you can't know what the client's hour costs, stay in hours. «It saves you 40 hours a month» is a sentence that works just as well and doesn't require you to guess salaries.

tasks.title: Work out what it actually costs you
tasks.action: Write the hours for four items separately: understanding their situation and their particulars, adapting the setup, training whoever will use it, and support for the first three months. Add them up. And now compare that total with what you'd have said off the top of your head before doing this breakdown.
tasks.expect: A total, and almost certainly a surprise. What's usual is that understanding, training and supporting add up to more than building.
tasks.stuck: If you've never done it for someone else and can't estimate, use the rule of three times your instinct. And note the real hours when you do it: the second time you'll have your own data.

tasks.title: Write your quote in three figures
tasks.action: Draft the quote with the three items separated: set-up (one-off payment), monthly cost of the tools (in the client's name, and say so), and monthly maintenance with what it includes. Underneath, in the same size type, the list of what it doesn't include.
tasks.prompt:
PROPOSAL · [PROJECT NAME]

WHAT IT SOLVES: [one sentence with the number it saves]

1. SET-UP: [amount] (one-off payment)
   Includes: [analysis, build, testing, training for X people, documentation]

2. TOOLS: approx. [amount] per month
   In the client's name. I don't charge this amount.

3. MAINTENANCE: [amount] per month
   Includes: [monthly review, warnings, breakdowns fixed within X hours]

DOESN'T INCLUDE (quoted separately):
- [New features]
- [Integration with other systems]
- [Training new staff after X months]
- [Changes of scope once approved]

TIMESCALE: [weeks]
WHAT I NEED FROM YOU: [access, documents, one point of contact]
tasks.expect: A one-page document with three figures. That last line, what you need from the client, prevents half the delays.
tasks.stuck: If the number embarrasses you, put it next to what you save them per month. If you save them 40 hours a month and the set-up costs what 20 hours cost, that's an easy conversation to have.

tasks.title: Have the AI find the holes in your quote
tasks.action: Give it your quote and ask it to play a client trying to take advantage, not an adviser.
tasks.prompt:
I'm giving you a quote of mine for an AI automation project. I want you to play a sharp client who's going to try to fit as much as possible inside the fixed price.

QUOTE:
[PASTE YOURS]

1. Tell me what requests you could slip past me during the project by arguing that «it's obviously included». Give me the exact sentences you'd say.
2. Which parts of my «includes» are vague enough to be stretched. Point at the specific words.
3. What's missing from the «doesn't include» that's going to cause me trouble.
4. According to my quote, what happens if the project runs long through the client's fault (they don't send the data, they don't show up to meetings)? Am I covered?

Don't tell me whether the price is high or low. Only where the scope can be stretched.
tasks.expect: Three or four sentences you will genuinely be told, and the vague words in your document. The commonest: «training» without saying how many people or how many hours.
tasks.stuck: If it answers with negotiation advice, cut it short: «I don't want advice. Tell me which exact word in my quote can be stretched.»

tasks.title: See what it would cost you the second time
tasks.action: Go back over the four items from task 2 and mark which would drop if you built the same thing again for a similar client, with the handover package from lesson 45 already done. Work out the second-time total.
tasks.expect: Two totals: first time and second. If the gap is large, that's your reason for picking one kind of client and repeating rather than making every project different.
tasks.stuck: If the second time barely drops, look at why: usually it's that you haven't done the handover package, or that each client needs something too bespoke. The first is fixable; the second tells you that isn't your product.

tasks.title: Write your three reasons to say no
tasks.action: Write the three kinds of job you're going to turn down or turn into a paid diagnostic phase. Have the sentence ready too, so you don't have to improvise it in a meeting where someone is offering you money.
tasks.expect: Three reasons and one sentence. The most useful: «Before the full project I propose a diagnostic of X hours for Y, which comes off if we go ahead.»
tasks.stuck: If you struggle to think of reasons, use the four from the theory and pick the three that frighten you most. And add one of your own if you've already had a bad experience: that's the most valuable one.

matters: That charging by your hours means earning less the better you get.
That building it for someone else includes understanding, adapting, training and supporting, and that usually weighs more than building.
That a quote is three separate figures and a list of what it doesn't include.
That the handover package from lesson 45 is what makes the second sale cost a quarter.
ignore: Average industry rates. Your price comes from what you save and what it costs you.
Dropping the price to land the first client. Drop the scope, not the price.
Promising short timescales to convince. Missed deadlines cost more than a high price.
canDo: Set a price with two numbers behind it rather than by eye.
Write what it doesn't include before the argument turns up.
Know how much the second sale drops and why.
cantDo: Know how long it'll take if you've never done it for someone else: that's why you multiply.
Stop a client trying to stretch the scope: only have it in writing.
Sell the same thing twice without having done the handover package.
Charge properly for a job whose problem isn't defined.
words: The one-off payment for leaving it working. Includes analysis, build, testing and training.
The monthly amount for watching it and fixing breakdowns. You say what it includes and within what time.
What's inside the price. Stretching it without charging is what ruins a well-paid project.
A small paid first job to define the problem before committing to a price.
Building the same thing for another client. It costs far less if the handover package is done.
next: You know how to package it, tell it, defend it and charge for it. Lesson 49 closes the course: how to choose the project you're actually going to do and how to finish it, which is the part where almost everyone falls down.
